title: JERICHO’S WALLS FELL… SO WHY DID GOD ALLOW ISRAEL TO BLEED AT AI?
paragraphs: JERICHO’S WALLS FELL… SO WHY DID GOD ALLOW ISRAEL TO BLEED AT AI?
The terrifying secret buried beneath a victorious army, the sin nobody wanted exposed, and the astonishing mercy of a God who can turn the very valley of judgment into a doorway of hope.
Jericho had fallen.
The walls were gone. The enemy was defeated. The impossible had happened.
And somewhere among the victorious Israelites, a man was hiding something that would soon cost lives.
Nobody knew.
Not the soldiers celebrating. Not the families waiting for their husbands to return. Not even Joshua, the leader who had just witnessed one of the greatest miracles in Israel's history.
But God knew.

And before long, thirty-six men would be dead, an entire nation would be trembling, and Joshua would be lying face down before the Ark of the Covenant, asking why the Lord had brought His people across the Jordan only to let them be defeated.
Here is the question that should make every believer uncomfortable:
How can a people who just witnessed an extraordinary miracle suffer a devastating defeat almost immediately afterward?
And an even deeper question...
What if the greatest danger to your spiritual life isn't the enemy standing in front of you, but the disobedience you've learned to hide behind you?
This is not simply the story of why Ai was destroyed after Jericho.

It is the story of what happens when victory becomes presumption, when hidden sin fractures a community, when judgment reveals the holiness of God, and when grace opens a future that failure seemed to have destroyed.
And if you've ever celebrated God's goodness while quietly struggling with something you hoped nobody would discover, you may recognize yourself somewhere in this story.
Because the road from Jericho to Ai passes through places in the human heart that many of us would rather avoid.
Jericho was not an ordinary military victory.
According to Joshua 6, Israel marched around the fortified city in obedience to God's instructions. On the seventh day, the people shouted, the priests blew their trumpets, and the wall fell.
The victory belonged to the Lord.
Israel had not conquered Jericho through superior siege engineering or overwhelming military power. The narrative emphasizes God's intervention and Israel's obedient faith.
But the victory came with a solemn command.

Jericho and its contents were placed under what Scripture calls חֵרֶם (ḥērem), a Hebrew term associated with something devoted to God, often through irrevocable destruction in the context of divine judgment.
This is a difficult concept for modern readers, and it should not be softened into something sentimental.
Joshua 6:17–19 distinguishes between what was devoted to destruction and the silver, gold, bronze, and iron that were to be placed in the treasury of the Lord.
Israel was not permitted to treat Jericho as an opportunity for personal enrichment.
The city was not theirs to plunder according to their own desires.
The victory was God's, and His instructions governed what happened afterward.
Then comes one of the most chilling transitions in the book of Joshua.
Joshua 7:1, in the King James Version, begins:
"But the children of Israel committed a trespass in the accursed thing..."
That single word, but, changes the atmosphere.
The walls had fallen.
The people had shouted.
The promise had been fulfilled.
But something was wrong.
A man named Achan, from the tribe of Judah, had taken items that God had forbidden Israel to take for themselves.
And although one man committed the act, the biblical narrator describes Israel as having broken faith.
The Hebrew expression וַיִּמְעֲלוּ בְנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל מַעַל (vayimʿalu vene-Yisra'el maʿal) conveys the idea that the children of Israel acted unfaithfully, committing a breach of trust.
This is more than a minor procedural violation.
In the covenant setting of Joshua, it was an act of unfaithfulness against the God who had delivered them.
And here is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Achan did not stand before the entire nation and announce his rebellion.
He hid it.
He carried the forbidden items into his tent and buried them beneath the ground.
Above the earth, everything may have appeared normal.
Beneath it lay evidence of disobedience.
How many people know what that feels like?
You worship publicly, but privately you are struggling.
You encourage others to trust God while wrestling with your own compromises.
You know the right words. You remember the Scriptures. You may even have testimonies of extraordinary things God has done in your life.
But there is a place you don't want Him to touch.
A conversation you keep returning to.
A dishonest practice you've justified.
A bitterness you've fed.
A secret you've convinced yourself is too small to matter.
Not every private struggle is deliberate rebellion, and temptation itself is not the same as sin. But when we knowingly protect disobedience, the story of Achan confronts our excuses.
Because a hidden thing is never hidden from God.
The Lord sees the entire person, including the places where shame and self-deception have built their little shelters.
And what happens next in Joshua 7 reveals just how dangerous spiritual presumption can become.
After Jericho, Joshua sent men to examine Ai, a city near Beth-aven, east of Bethel.
The spies returned with confidence.
Ai was small compared with Jericho. There was no need to send the entire army. Two or three thousand soldiers should be sufficient.
They had seen God bring down Jericho.
Surely Ai would be easy.
But Israel's next battle ended in disaster.
The men of Ai struck down about thirty-six Israelites and pursued the others, leaving the people terrified.
Joshua 7:5 describes the nation's courage collapsing.
The Hebrew expression וַיְהִי לְמָיִם (vayehi lemayim) means, literally, that their heart became like water.
The people who had crossed the Jordan on dry ground now felt their courage dissolve.
Think about the families of those thirty-six men.
Thirty-six households facing a loss they had not expected.
Thirty-six lives that would never return from what had been considered a manageable battle.
These were not anonymous pieces on a theological chessboard.
They were human beings.
And Scripture refuses to present their deaths as a trivial matter.
Joshua tore his clothes and fell before the Ark of the Lord until evening.
He questioned what had happened.
Why had God brought Israel across the Jordan if they were going to be destroyed?
What would happen to the Lord's great name?
Joshua was devastated.
Then came the answer.
In Joshua 7:10–11, God commanded Joshua to rise and revealed that Israel had sinned by violating His covenant, taking devoted things, stealing, deceiving, and concealing what had been taken.
The defeat was not evidence that the Lord had become weaker than the gods of Canaan.
It was evidence that Israel could not presume upon His presence while disregarding His command.
Yesterday's victory was never permission for today's disobedience.
That sentence deserves to settle deeply in the heart.
Because sometimes we confuse God's past faithfulness with an assurance that our present choices have no consequences.
We remember the prayer He answered.
The relationship He restored.
The sickness through which He sustained us.
The door He opened when there seemed to be no way forward.
And slowly, almost imperceptibly, gratitude can turn into entitlement.
We begin acting as though yesterday's miracle makes obedience optional today.
But the God who brought down Jericho's walls was still holy when Israel approached Ai.
His character had not changed.
The problem was not that God had abandoned His covenant promises.
The problem was that His people had violated the covenant.
Yet we must be careful here.

Joshua 7 describes a particular covenant judgment at a particular moment in Israel's history. It does not give Christians permission to assume that every financial hardship, illness, bereavement, or disappointment is punishment for hidden sin.
Jesus Himself rejected that simplistic reasoning in John 9:1–3 when His disciples assumed that a man's blindness must have resulted from someone's sin.
Sometimes suffering is connected to wrongdoing.
Sometimes it is not.
We are not authorized to diagnose another person's pain as divine punishment.
But we are called to examine our own hearts before God.
And that is precisely where Joshua's story leads us.
God instructed Joshua to consecrate the people.
The next morning, the nation was brought forward in a process of identification, until Achan was singled out.
Joshua urged him to acknowledge what he had done.
And at last, the truth came into the light.
Achan confessed that he had seen a beautiful Babylonian garment, two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing fifty shekels.
Then he described the progression of his sin.
He saw.
He coveted.
He took.
He hid.
In Joshua 7:21, the sequence is devastating because it is so recognizable.
Sin often begins long before anyone notices its outward consequences.
A glance becomes a desire.
A desire becomes a justification.
A justification becomes a decision.
And a decision becomes a secret that must be protected.
The Hebrew verb חָמַד (ḥāmad), used in Achan's confession, means to desire or covet. It recalls the prohibition against coveting in the Ten Commandments.
Achan's failure was not merely that he possessed the wrong objects.
He allowed desire to override God's explicit command.
And the terrible irony is that the man who secretly took treasure from Jericho ended up losing far more than he gained.
The stolen goods were found beneath his tent, exactly where he had concealed them.
The judgment that followed is among the most disturbing scenes in the Old Testament.

Joshua 7:24–26 recounts Achan's removal to the Valley of Achor, together with the devoted items, his possessions, and members of his household. The account describes the execution of judgment, including stoning and burning, and the raising of a great heap of stones.
The text is severe.
It raises painful questions about collective responsibility, the involvement of Achan's household, and the administration of judgment under Israel's ancient covenant.
Faithful readers should not pretend those questions are easy.
The narrative does not give us every detail about the knowledge or culpability of each household member, and interpreters differ on precisely how to understand their involvement.
What Scripture clearly presents is a grave covenant violation followed by a grave judgment.
This episode is not an instruction for Christians to punish sinners through violence.
The church is not ancient Israel's covenant army, and the New Testament does not authorize believers to reproduce Joshua's conquest judgments.
Our calling is to proclaim Christ, practice truth, pursue holiness, exercise appropriate spiritual accountability, and extend the invitation of repentance and forgiveness.
Yet we must not miss the warning.
Sin promises to give us something worth hiding, then demands more than we ever intended to surrender.
And perhaps that is the part of this story that hurts most.
Achan finally confessed.
But his confession came after exposure, and it did not erase the earthly consequences of his actions.
This is not because repentance is meaningless.
It is because forgiveness and consequences are not the same thing.
A person may truly repent and still need to repair what was damaged, face legitimate accountability, or endure the consequences of previous choices.
Grace is not a denial of reality.
It is God's merciful answer to sinners who cannot save themselves.
But now comes a question that many readers overlook.
If Joshua 7 explains why Israel lost at Ai, why did God command Israel to return and destroy the city in Joshua 8?
Because Ai was not destroyed simply to punish Achan's sin.
Achan's judgment and Ai's destruction are related within the story, but they are not the same event and do not have the same immediate purpose.
After the covenant violation was addressed, God renewed His command for Israel to advance against Ai.
Joshua 8:1 records the Lord telling Joshua not to be afraid or dismayed, and promising to give the king of Ai, his people, his city, and his land into Israel's hand.
The campaign against Ai belongs to the larger conquest narrative, in which Israel is entering the land God had promised to Abraham's descendants.

Deuteronomy 9:4–5 explicitly warns Israel not to interpret possession of the land as proof of its own righteousness. The passage connects the displacement of the nations with their wickedness and with God's promises to the patriarchs.

Genesis 15:16 had already described the iniquity of the Amorites as not yet complete, indicating that the biblical story presents divine judgment as neither arbitrary nor disconnected from a larger history.
Still, these explanations do not remove the moral weight of the account.
Joshua 8 describes the destruction of Ai's inhabitants, including the killing of twelve thousand men and women according to verse 25.
We should not celebrate that loss of life as though it were entertainment.
The biblical narrative presents it as judgment within a specific, ancient, redemptive-historical setting, not as a universal model for religious conquest.
Christians read these events in the light of Jesus Christ, who forbade His disciples from advancing His kingdom by the sword and commanded them to make disciples of all nations.
The Lord who judges evil is also the Lord who calls sinners to repentance.
And the New Testament declares that the risen Christ will judge the world in righteousness.
God's holiness and mercy are not competing personalities.
They belong to the same perfectly righteous God.
But something else changed between the first and second battles at Ai.
And it is a detail that reveals how carefully we must listen to Scripture.
At Jericho, Israel had been forbidden to take the devoted goods for personal use.
At Ai, God expressly permitted the Israelites to take the livestock and spoil for themselves, according to Joshua 8:2.
Read that again.
What Achan had grasped unlawfully at Jericho, Israel was permitted to receive under God's instructions at Ai.
That does not mean the two sets of goods were identical or that Achan would personally have received the treasure he coveted.
But the contrast is striking.
Achan seized what God had forbidden, while the army later received what God had permitted.
How often does impatience persuade us to violate a command because we cannot bear to wait?
We want the relationship before commitment.
The reward before integrity.
The promotion without honesty.
The satisfaction without surrender.
We reach for something outside God's will because we fear obedience will leave us empty-handed.
Yet Scripture repeatedly warns that gaining what we desire at the expense of faithfulness is no true victory.
Jesus asks in Mark 8:36 what it profits a person to gain the whole world and lose his own soul.
That question reaches far beyond the ancient battlefield.
You can gain the applause and lose your peace.
Gain the money and compromise your integrity.
Gain the appearance of holiness while becoming increasingly distant from honest fellowship with God.
And perhaps the saddest possibility of all is to hold something tightly that was never worth the cost of your disobedience.
When Israel returned to Ai, the battle unfolded differently.
Joshua followed the Lord's instructions and employed an ambush.
Part of the Israelite force drew Ai's defenders away from the city. Another force entered and set it on fire. The army of Ai was caught between Israelite forces, and the city was defeated.
The first attack had ended with Israel fleeing.
The second ended with Ai's army overwhelmed.
But the deeper turning point occurred before the military maneuver.
The covenant violation had been confronted, and the Lord had instructed Israel to proceed.
Israel's renewed success was not a formula by which repentance mechanically guarantees military or material victory.
It was the fulfillment of God's specific promise to Joshua in that moment.
And the chapter does not end with a celebration of military superiority.
It ends with worship and the Word of God.
Joshua built an altar to the Lord on Mount Ebal, as Moses had commanded.
He wrote a copy of the law and read its words before the assembly of Israel, including women, children, and foreigners living among them.
Joshua 8:35 emphasizes that nothing Moses had commanded was omitted from the reading before the gathered community.
Consider the contrast.
The nation that had suffered because of covenant unfaithfulness was now standing together to hear the covenant's words.
The people who had trembled in defeat were gathered before the Lord.
Their future was not to be built on self-confidence, military reputation, or the memory of Jericho.
It was to be shaped by God's Word.
And that brings us to one of the most extraordinary connections in the entire account.
The place where Achan was judged was called the Valley of Achor.
The Hebrew word עָכוֹר (ʿākhor) is associated with trouble or disturbance.
Joshua 7:26 connects the name with the trouble Achan brought upon Israel.
It was a place marked by judgment, loss, and painful remembrance.
But the story of that valley does not end in Joshua.
Centuries later, the prophet Hosea speaks of God's intention to restore His unfaithful people.
In Hosea 2:15, the Lord declares, in the King James Version:
"And I will give her her vineyards from thence, and the valley of Achor for a door of hope..."
A door of hope.
The valley associated with trouble becomes, in God's promise of restoration, a doorway of hope.
The Hebrew expression פֶּתַח תִּקְוָה (petaḥ tiqvah) means an opening or doorway of hope.
This is not Hosea denying the judgment that occurred in Joshua.
It is the prophet announcing God's power to bring covenant restoration where the memory of judgment once stood.
And now the story begins to speak with astonishing force to the wounded human heart.
Because some of us know what it means to live in a valley named Trouble.
Maybe yours has a different name.
Divorce.
Betrayal.
Addiction.
Dishonesty.
A shattered family.
A ministry failure.
A season of rebellion.
A secret you finally confessed.
A consequence you cannot reverse.
A person you hurt and cannot make everything right with again.
You look backward and wish you could change one decision.
One conversation.
One night.
One compromise.
And somewhere inside, a terrible sentence keeps repeating:
I ruined everything.
But listen carefully.
The Gospel does not promise that every earthly consequence will disappear.
It does not guarantee that every relationship will be restored exactly as it was, or that every lost opportunity will return.
And it does not pretend that those we have harmed should simply forget what happened.
What the Gospel announces is greater than denial.
Through Jesus Christ, your sin does not have to be the final word over your relationship with God.
This is where the story must lead us.
Not merely back to Joshua.
Not merely back to Ai.
But forward to the cross of Jesus Christ.
Because the deepest human problem is not that we sometimes lose battles.
It is that we are sinners before a holy God.
Romans 3:23 declares:
"For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God."
Achan's story exposes something universal.
Human beings are capable of desiring what God forbids, hiding what they have done, and hoping the truth will never come to light.
Some sins are public.
Others are carefully concealed.
Some are condemned by society.
Others are applauded.
But none of us can stand before God and claim to have lived in perfect obedience.
And if the story ended with human guilt and divine judgment, there would be no lasting hope.
But the Gospel announces that Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He did not grasp what was forbidden.
He did not betray His calling.
He did not conceal a sinful life beneath religious appearances.
He was the sinless Son of God.
And yet He went to the cross.
Not because He had sinned.
But to accomplish redemption for sinners.
Second Corinthians 5:21 declares:
"For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him."
This does not mean Jesus became morally sinful.
It means that the sinless Christ bore sin's burden in His saving work, so that those united to Him by faith might receive righteousness before God.
And Galatians 3:13 says that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.
The apostle Paul draws upon the language of Deuteronomy 21:23, connecting the shame of one hanged on a tree with Christ's crucifixion.
The connection between Joshua's story and the cross is not that Jesus is simply another Achan or that the two events are identical.
Achan was guilty.
Jesus was innocent.
Achan's actions brought trouble upon Israel.
Jesus willingly gave Himself to redeem His people.
The ancient judgment reveals the seriousness of sin.
The cross reveals both the seriousness of sin and the immeasurable grace of God.
At Calvary, divine justice was not dismissed as irrelevant.
And mercy was not withheld from all who would believe.
Jesus died and rose again.
He is not merely an example of someone who endured suffering.
He is the crucified and risen Savior who offers forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life.
That is why repentance is not simply feeling terrible about the past.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated repentance, speaks of a change of mind or heart that involves turning from sin toward God.
Biblical repentance is not a performance designed to earn forgiveness.
It is the fitting response of a sinner who hears God's truth, turns away from rebellion, and comes to Christ in faith.
First John 1:9 gives believers this assurance:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because God has forgotten His holiness.
But because Jesus Christ is the righteous Advocate and atoning Savior described in the very next chapter.
There is something deeply moving about that.
The God who sees what you hide is also the God who calls you to come into the light.
You do not have to manufacture an innocent past.
You do not have to pretend the damage never happened.
You do not have to defend what the Lord is calling you to surrender.
You can confess.
You can repent.
You can seek forgiveness.
You can begin making things right where possible.
And you can trust the Savior who receives those who come to Him.
John 6:37 records Jesus saying:
"Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out."
Perhaps you have been avoiding prayer because you are ashamed.
Perhaps you still attend church, but your heart has grown cold.
Perhaps you can speak confidently about Scripture while privately knowing that your relationship with God needs honest attention.
Or perhaps you are not yet a Christian, and you have assumed that your history makes you too damaged for Christ.
Hear this clearly.
You cannot save yourself by hiding your sin.
You cannot purchase forgiveness through religious activity.
And you cannot undo yesterday by pretending it never happened.
But you can come to Jesus.
Right now.
Not when you have perfected yourself.
Not when your reputation has recovered.
Not when every consequence has disappeared.
Come in repentance and faith.
The Savior who died for sinners is alive.
And His grace is not reserved for people with spotless histories.
This is the heart of what we mean at Gospel Warrior when we say:
We do not mean that Jesus changes the historical facts of what happened.
We mean that through His redeeming work, guilt can meet forgiveness, shame can give way to a new identity in Christ, and a broken life can be transformed by the power of the Holy Spirit.
The scandal does not become good.
The sin does not become righteous.
The victims do not become unimportant.
But Jesus can redeem sinners and give them a future that their past could never have earned.
And if this article has uncovered something you've been carrying, I want to invite you to respond with honesty.
You don't need to tell strangers every detail of your private struggle.
But you don't have to pretend you're untouched either.
Not as a performance.
Not to impress anyone.
But as a small, sincere acknowledgment that we all need the mercy of God.
Someone reading your words may discover that they are not the only person fighting to remain faithful.
Someone may find the courage to seek help, confess a sin, or return to prayer.
And someone who has been hiding behind a polished religious image may finally understand that the Gospel calls us not to pretend, but to come to Christ.
If this message made you think of a friend, a brother, a sister, or someone who has quietly drifted away from God, consider sharing it with them.
A simple share can place Scripture before someone who may never intentionally search for a Christian message.

You may never know who reads it during a lonely night, who saves it to revisit after a difficult conversation, or who finds encouragement to open the Bible again because you cared enough to pass it along.
Not because every word here must be remembered, but because Joshua 7–8 deserves more than a hurried reading.
Return to the passages.
Examine the context.
Read the difficult verses.
Test the explanations against Scripture.
Let God's Word, not merely the emotions of a story, shape your convictions.
Our desire is to keep pointing people to Jesus Christ through Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, biblical truth, spiritual encouragement, and practical discipleship.
We also want to make that journey deeper than a single Facebook article.
These resources are part of our commitment to helping people grow beyond momentary inspiration into a more mature, grounded, Christ-centered faith.
And for those who believe in this mission and have the means to help sustain it, I want to extend a personal invitation.
It is not a condition of salvation.
It does not make you more righteous than someone who cannot afford to give.
And it should never replace the faithful financial responsibilities you have toward your local church, family, or those in need.
Rather, it is an opportunity to participate voluntarily in a ministry of biblical encouragement and discipleship.

Scripture teaches that believers may generously support those who labor to share God's Word. Galatians 6:6 speaks of sharing good things with those who teach, and 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should be willing, not reluctant or compelled.
Not because we can measure their love for God by a payment.
But because faithful, willing generosity can help make sound biblical teaching and encouragement accessible to more people.
These items can serve as reminders of biblical truth, thoughtful gifts, or practical tools for reflection and study.
It is the opportunity to help sustain a mission centered on making Christ known.
The invitation to read Scripture, seek Christ, receive encouragement, and grow in the knowledge of God's Word is not reserved for paying supporters.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Jesus Christ is the treasure.
Everything we do should point toward Him.
And before you leave, I want you to think once more about Joshua.
He had watched Jericho's walls fall.
He had experienced the humiliation of Ai.
He had fallen before God in anguish.
He had confronted a painful truth.
And then he had heard the Lord tell him to rise and move forward.
Not because Israel's failure had never happened.
But because God's purposes were not finished.
Maybe you needed that reminder today.
You cannot go back and become someone who never sinned.
You cannot rebuild yesterday exactly as it was.
You cannot make every scar disappear.
But through Jesus Christ, you can receive forgiveness, walk in repentance, and live a new life by His grace.
Turn to Christ.
Believe the Gospel.
Bring Him the truth about your sin and your need for mercy.
Ask Him to teach you obedience, restore what can rightly be restored, and lead you into the life that only He can give.
Because the greatest miracle in this story is not that Jericho's walls collapsed.
Nor is it that Israel eventually conquered Ai.
It is the larger biblical truth to which these events direct our attention: the holy God who judges sin has opened the way of salvation through His Son.
And even the Valley of Achor, once remembered as a place of trouble, could become a prophetic doorway of hope.
The place where your sin was exposed does not have to be the place where your story ends—because the Savior who knows your darkest chapter still calls repentant sinners into His marvelous light.
